items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's Narumi print shows shopfronts hung with lengths of patterned cloth: Arimatsu shibori. The craft dates from 1608, when the Owari domain founded Arimatsu on the highway just east of Narumi; Takeda Shōkurō is credited with starting it there. Travelers bought tie-dyed towels and summer kimono as souvenirs, and both towns grew prosperous on the trade.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō ed.), Narumi 'Meibutsu Arimatsu shibori'

items.bodyEn: 絞 pairs 糸, thread, with 交, to cross or intertwine, and the Shuowen Jiezi glosses it as binding tight, as a cord binds a neck. From that come 絞る, to wring or squeeze, and 絞り, cloth bound, stitched and twisted so that dye cannot reach the tied parts. Each knot leaves a pale ring once the thread is cut away.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 絞 (縊也、从交从糸); Daijisen, entry 絞り

items.bodyEn: After a verb stem, 得る means 'can happen' or 'can be done' and is read either うる or える: あり得る is ありうる or ありえる. The older うる sounds more formal and is the usual choice in writing. The negative, though, is always 得ない, read えない: ありえない, never ありうない. This station's 〜ざるを得ない is a fixed form read ざるをえない.

In the winter of 1687 Matsuo Bashō stayed with poets in Narumi and opened a linked-verse session with this hokku: plovers crying as if to say, look at the darkness over Hoshizaki. His hosts raised a stone, the Chidorizuka, carved from his own handwriting, and it is regarded as the only Bashō monument set up during his lifetime.
items.ja: {星崎|ほしざき}の{闇|やみ}を{見|み}よとや{啼|な}く{千鳥|ちどり}
items.kana: ほしざきのやみをみよとやなくちどり
items.sourceNote: Bashō, hokku of the Narumi kasen (1687); Chidorizuka monument, Narumi
